intro: Histogram height and histogram probability are different quantities when bin widths vary. A density must be multiplied by bin width to recover its probability mass.
task: Accumulate nonnegative sample weights into uneven bins and divide by total weight and bin widths.
requirements: values and nonnegative weights have equal lengths; weights have positive total. edges is strictly increasing with gaps at least 1e-6 and covers every value.
Bins are [left,right), except the final bin includes its right endpoint. Return {"mass": normalized weight per bin, "density": mass/bin_width}.

Unless a requirement explicitly sets another range, numeric inputs are real and finite with magnitude at most 10000. Booleans are rejected except explicit boolean masks. Vectors have length 1..64 and matrix axes 1..64 unless specified otherwise. Leave inputs unchanged. Raise ValueError for invalid types, bounds, shapes or documented domain conditions.

examples.name: Uneven bin widths
examples.output:
{'mass': [0.1666666667, 0.8333333333], 'density': [0.1666666667, 0.2777777778]}
(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 10 significant digits.)

examples.name: Right endpoint
examples.output:
{'mass': [0.0, 1.0], 'density': [0.0, 1.0]}
(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 10 significant digits.)

examples.name: Zero weight
examples.output:
{'mass': [0.0, 1.0], 'density': [0.0, 0.5]}
(NumPy arrays shown as lists; rounded to 10 significant digits.)

hints.title: Choose the representation
hints.body: Assign interior-edge values to the bin on their right, with a special inclusive final endpoint.

hints.title: Build the result
hints.body: Normalize weighted counts into masses before dividing by each bin width.

explanation: Histogram height and histogram probability are different quantities when bin widths vary. A density must be multiplied by bin width to recover its probability mass.
Nonnegative weights can represent repeated observations or unequal importance. Their total, rather than the number of values, is the normalizing constant; zero-weight samples contribute no mass.
